subject: math

unit.title: Calculation: add, subtract, multiply, divide
unit.essentialQuestion: How do we add and take away bigger numbers, and what does 'lots of' mean?

title: Retrieval & fluency: calculation
objectives: By the end, I can quickly add/subtract two-digit numbers and recall 2/5/10 facts.

vocabulary.definition: a quick sensible guess made BEFORE solving
swap ten ones for a ten (or a ten for ten ones)
vocabulary.example: 8 + 7 = 15 → exchange ten ones for a ten

vocabulary.definition: the operation that undoes another — used to check
a times-table answer you recall from memory
fast AND accurate — strong maths muscles

emphasize: This is a fluency WORKOUT — speed and accuracy together. No new idea today: it's all retrieval.
The routine for every question: ESTIMATE, SOLVE, CHECK. The estimate is the safety net that catches silly answers.
Mix the strands (add, subtract, times, divide) so the child must CHOOSE the right method each time.

misconceptions: skipping the estimate, so wild answers go unnoticed
regrouping slips under time pressure (forgetting the exchanged ten)
confusing operations in mixed practice (30 ÷ 10 answered as 300 or 20)
not using the inverse to check — treating checking as extra work
hooks: Maths Gym Day — let's flex every muscle we've built!
priorKnowledge: everything from Unit 2: regrouping add/subtract (L6–7), inverse (L8), arrays (L9), tables (L10), division (L11)

digital: train-track progress relay (one station per correct answer)
number line and base-10 visuals as backup tools

plan.goal: Set the gym-day energy; warm up with a skip-count; retrieve why we estimate.
plan.note: High energy, zero new content. The train-track relay is introduced here: every correct answer moves the train one station.
plan.successCriteria: Child skip-counts in 5s to 30 and says an estimate 'checks the answer makes sense'.

script.say: It's Maths Gym Day! This unit you've built serious maths muscles — adding, taking away, times tables, sharing. Today we flex ALL of them, and every correct answer moves your train one station down the track. Warm-up first: count in 5s to 30 — go! … Lovely. Now, brain question: what's the first thing a good mathematician does before solving — a rough guess. Why?
script.adaptHints: Swap the train for the child's favourite vehicle or creature journeying along the track. Listen for 'to check the answer makes sense'.

blocks.caption: Every correct answer moves the train one station!

stuckProtocol: If the skip-count stalls: count in 5s together with fingers, one finger per jump.

plan.goal: Model the estimate–solve–check routine once, on 48 + 37 — light and quick, no new maths.
plan.note: Review lesson: this 'explain' only models the ROUTINE. Think aloud, fast and confident.
plan.successCriteria: Child hears the full routine — estimate ~90, solve 85, check against the estimate — and can name its three steps.

script.say: Here's our gym routine for every single question: ESTIMATE, SOLVE, CHECK. Watch me do one rep. 48 + 37. Estimate first: that's about 50 and 40 — around 90. Solve: ones first — 8 + 7 = 15, that's a ten and 5, exchange! Tens: 40 + 30 + my new ten = 80. Answer: 85. Check: is 85 close to my estimate of 90? Yes — makes sense! Say the three steps with me: estimate… solve… check!
script.adaptHints: Keep it brisk — this is a warm-up demo, not a teach. Let the child shout the three steps.

plan.goal: Child runs the routine on 71 − 26, then flexes the tables/division link with 6 × 5 → 30 ÷ 5.
plan.note: The child leads; the character only prompts the next step of the routine.
plan.successCriteria: Child estimates ~45–50, solves 71 − 26 = 45 with the exchange, and answers 6 × 5 = 30 then 30 ÷ 5 = 6, naming them inverses.

script.say: Your turn on the machines! 71 − 26. Step one — estimate: roughly 70 take away 30 is about…? Now solve — careful, are there enough ones? You'll need to break a ten. … 45! Does that sit near your estimate? Now a tables superset: 6 × 5? … And if 6 × 5 = 30, then 30 ÷ 5 is…? See — they're inverses, one undoes the other!
script.adaptHints: If the exchange stumbles, slow down just that step: '1 take away 6 — not enough — break a ten: 71 becomes 60 and 11.'

wrongAnswers.why: subtracted 5 instead of dividing — ÷ read as −
wrongAnswers.remedy: 30 ÷ 5 asks how many 5s are in 30 — you JUST said six 5s make 30!

wrongAnswers.why: added instead of multiplied
wrongAnswers.remedy: Six GROUPS of 5 — skip-count: 5, 10, 15…

plan.goal: Diagnostic: mixed-operation recall (30 ÷ 10) plus using the inverse to PROVE an answer.
plan.note: Two-part check straight from the script. The inverse proof is the deeper diagnostic — checking must feel like power, not chores.
plan.successCriteria: Child answers 30 ÷ 10 = 3 and explains that 85 − 37 = 48 proves 48 + 37 = 85.

script.say: Checkpoint! First: 30 ÷ 10. … Now the detective one: earlier we found 48 + 37 = 85. Prove it's right using a SUBTRACTION. Which subtraction should we do, and where should it land?
script.adaptHints: After a correct proof, probe: 'how does that check prove it?' Listen for 'take a part away from the whole and you must land on the other part'.

options: 85 − 37 = 48 — take a part from the whole, land on the other part
blocks.explain: The whole is 85. Take away one part (37) and you must land exactly on the other part (48). If you don't, the sum was wrong.

check.question: Solve 30 ÷ 10, then prove 48 + 37 = 85 using subtraction.
check.expectedAnswer: 3; and 85 − 37 = 48, so the sum is right

wrongAnswers.why: confused the operation — subtracted or multiplied instead
wrongAnswers.remedy: How many 10s in 30? Skip-count: 10, 20, 30 — how many jumps?

wrongAnswers.why: part-whole link not used — checking feels like new work
wrongAnswers.remedy: The whole is 85. Take a part, 37, away — where SHOULD you land if the sum was right?

plan.goal: The main workout: interleaved quick-fire across all Unit 2 skills, estimate-solve-check each time, train advancing per correct answer.
plan.note: Director draws from the practiceBank, start level 2, deliberately ALTERNATING strands (add → times → subtract → divide → inverse…) so the child chooses the method. Every correct answer moves the train. Keep pace brisk; backup tools only on a miss.
plan.successCriteria: Child completes 5+ mixed items mostly correct, estimating before each calculation and using one inverse check.

script.say: Main workout — the relay! I'll mix everything: adding, taking away, times, sharing. Estimate, solve, check, and the train rolls one station every time you're right. If a muscle wobbles, we grab a tool, fix it, and roll on. Ready? Wheels rolling!
script.adaptHints: Narrate the train's journey with the child's interests (dragon flying between castles, rocket between planets). Never change the numbers.

stuckProtocol: Name why: slip vs missing fact vs wrong operation.
Hand over the backup tool for that one item — number line for facts, drawn base-10 for regrouping.
One hint or a sentence starter ('ones first…', 'how many 5s in…').
Re-ask a smaller version, then build back up.
Keep it safe: 'Mistakes show us what to practise — smaller step.'

plan.goal: Honest self-assessment: strongest muscle and the one needing more gym time; end on a win.
plan.note: The child's named weak strand becomes the next lesson's warm-up. Record it.
plan.successCriteria: Child names one strong strand and one to practise, honestly.

script.say: Cool-down time, athlete! Look back at the track — what a journey. Tell me: which maths muscle felt STRONGEST today — adding, taking away, times tables or sharing? … And which one needs more gym time? … That's a champion's answer — knowing what to train next is how you get stronger. And you estimated before every answer — that's why the silly mistakes nearly vanished!
script.adaptHints: Whatever strand the child names as weak, respond warmly and store it for the next warm-up — never treat it as a failure.

wrongAnswers.why: added tens to tens but muddled the ones (3 + 4 slip)
wrongAnswers.remedy: Ones first: 3 + 4. Then tens: 20 + 10. Put the parts together.

wrongAnswers.why: added a digit into the wrong column
wrongAnswers.remedy: Line up tens under tens, ones under ones — which digits belong together?

reteach.say: Split both numbers: 23 is 20 and 3; 14 is 10 and 4. Tens together: 30. Ones together: 7. Recombine: 37 — and no exchanging needed this time.

wrongAnswers.why: added 2 + 5
wrongAnswers.remedy: Two GROUPS of 5 — jump twice: 5… 10.

wrongAnswers.why: grabbed 5 × 5 by mistake
wrongAnswers.remedy: Only TWO jumps of 5 — count them.

reteach.say: Two 5p coins: 5… 10. Two 5s make 10 — that one should pop out fast now!

block.explain: How many 2s in 10? Count: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 — five of them. And 5 × 2 = 10!

wrongAnswers.why: subtracted 2 — read ÷ as −
wrongAnswers.remedy: We're not taking 2 away — we're asking how many 2s FIT in 10. Count in 2s.

wrongAnswers.why: multiplied instead of divided
wrongAnswers.remedy: Dividing splits the number up — should the answer be bigger or smaller than 10?

reteach.say: Count the 2s hiding in 10 on your fingers: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 — five fingers up! 10 ÷ 2 = 5, because 5 × 2 = 10. The times table answers the division for free.

wrongAnswers.why: forgot the exchanged ten — classic regrouping slip
wrongAnswers.remedy: 6 + 8 = 14 — that's a ten AND a 4. Where did your new ten go? Add it with the tens.

wrongAnswers.why: wrote 14 whole instead of exchanging
wrongAnswers.remedy: 14 ones is too many for the ones seat — swap ten of them for a ten-rod first.

reteach.say: Estimate: 60 + 30 is about 90. Now solve: 6 + 8 = 14 — exchange ten ones for a ten, keep the 4. Tens: 50 + 20 + 10 = 80. Answer 84 — nice and close to 90, so it makes sense!

wrongAnswers.why: flipped the ones (did 9 − 4 'because you can't do 4 − 9')
wrongAnswers.remedy: You CAN — break a ten! 64 becomes 50 and 14. Now 14 − 9 is fine.

wrongAnswers.why: no estimate or inverse check used
wrongAnswers.remedy: Check it: 25 + 39 — do you land back on 64?

hints: Not enough ones? Break a ten: 64 → 50 and 14.

reteach.say: Estimate: about 60 − 40 = 20. Solve: 4 − 9 — not enough ones, so break a ten. 64 becomes 50 and 14. Now 14 − 9 = 5, and 50 − 30 = 20. Answer 25 — right next to the estimate. The exchange saves the day again!

wrongAnswers.why: added 7 + 5
wrongAnswers.remedy: Seven GROUPS of 5 — skip-count on fingers: 5, 10, 15…

wrongAnswers.why: one jump short (landed on 6 × 5)
wrongAnswers.remedy: Count your jumps on fingers — you need exactly seven fives.

hints: Start from 5 × 5 = 25 and jump two more fives.
The answer must end in 0 or 5.

reteach.say: Ladder trick: stand on 5 × 5 = 25, take two more jumps of 5 — 30, 35. So 7 × 5 = 35. Ends in 5 — correct uniform for the 5s!

wrongAnswers.why: subtracted 5 — read ÷ as −
wrongAnswers.remedy: How many 5s FIT in 25? Use the fact: ? × 5 = 25.

wrongAnswers.why: multiplied instead of divided
wrongAnswers.remedy: Dividing splits 25 into equal groups — can the answer be bigger than 25?

hints: Count in 5s to 25 — how many jumps?

reteach.say: The times table walks backwards: 5 × 5 = 25, so 25 ÷ 5 = 5. No counting needed when you own the fact!

block.prompt: You worked out 56 + 28 = 84. Which check PROVES it?
block.explain: Take a part (28) away from the whole (84) — you must land on the other part (56). You did, so the sum is right.

wrongAnswers.why: added again instead of undoing
wrongAnswers.remedy: A check must UNDO the operation. You added — so what undoes adding?

wrongAnswers.why: subtracted the parts from each other, not from the whole
wrongAnswers.remedy: Start from the WHOLE, 84. Take one part away — where should you land?

hints: Whole − one part = the other part.

reteach.say: Think part-part-whole: 56 and 28 are the parts, 84 is the whole. Take 28 off the whole and you MUST land back on 56 — if you don't, sound the alarm! That's the detective check.

block.prompt: Before solving 52 + 39, which is the BEST estimate?
block.explain: Round each number: 52 ≈ 50, 39 ≈ 40. 50 + 40 = 90 — so the real answer should land near 90.

wrongAnswers.why: over-rounded or added a stray ten
wrongAnswers.remedy: Round each number to its nearest ten first: 52 is close to…? 39 is close to…?

wrongAnswers.why: sees estimating as extra work, not a safety net
wrongAnswers.remedy: If you accidentally got 811, what would tell you something went wrong? That's the estimate's job!

hints: Round each number to the nearest ten.

reteach.say: The estimate is your safety net. Round: 52 is about 50, 39 is about 40 — together about 90. Now if your solved answer comes out at 91, brilliant. If it comes out at 811 — the net catches you!

block.title: How to estimate
steps: Round each number to the nearest ten: 52 → 50, 39 → 40
Solve properly, then check you landed NEAR 90

block.prompt: Word problem: 5 bags with 5 sweets in each. You eat 3 sweets. How many are left?

wrongAnswers.why: did the multiplication but forgot step two
wrongAnswers.remedy: Great start — 25 sweets! But then you ate 3. What happens next?

wrongAnswers.why: grabbed the numbers and added (5 + 5 − 3)
wrongAnswers.remedy: Act it out: 5 bags, 5 in EACH — is that 5 + 5 or 5 groups of 5?

hints: Two steps: first how many sweets altogether?
5 × 5 first… then take away the eaten ones.

reteach.say: Detective work — this story has TWO steps. Step one: 5 bags of 5 is 5 × 5 = 25 sweets. Step two: you ate 3, so 25 − 3 = 22. Read the story, spot the steps, solve them in order.

wrongAnswers.why: avoided the exchange — did 3 − 0 upside down
wrongAnswers.remedy: 0 − 3 needs a broken ten: 70 becomes 60 and 10. Now 10 − 3 works.

wrongAnswers.why: broke the ten but forgot the tens went down to 60
wrongAnswers.remedy: You broke a ten off 70 — so how many tens are LEFT before you subtract 20?

hints: 70 has no loose ones — break a ten: 60 and 10.

reteach.say: Estimate: about 70 − 20 = 50. Now the crunch: 70 has zero loose ones, so break a ten — 70 becomes 60 and 10. 10 − 3 = 7. 60 − 20 = 40. Answer 47, snuggled right by the estimate. Crossing a tens number is exactly when the exchange shines.

adaptivity.levelUp: 2 consecutive correct at the current level → next level; at level 3, run a timed streak — no tools, interleaving all four operations.
adaptivity.levelDown: 2 misses on the same skill → run that item's reteach with the backup tool visible (drawn base-10 for regrouping, number line for facts), then serve a level-1 item of that skill.
adaptivity.masterySignal: 6+ correct across levels 2–3 spanning at least three strands (add / subtract / tables / divide), each preceded by an estimate where relevant, plus one successful inverse check → mastery ≥ 0.8 for 'Unit 2 calculation fluency'.
struggleProtocol: Name why: slip vs missing fact vs wrong operation.
Hand over the backup tool for that one item (drawn blocks / number line).
One hint or sentence starter ('ones first…', 'how many 5s in…').
Re-ask a smaller version, then build back up.
Keep it safe: 'Mistakes show us what to practise — smaller step.'
adaptivity.personalization: Theme the relay track with the learner's interests (rocket between planets, dragon between castles); use their named weak strand from previous sessions to pick extra items. Never change the numbers.
adaptivity.endOnSuccess: Finish on a strand the child is strong in so the train reaches the final station on a win; process praise: 'you estimated before every answer — that's why the silly mistakes nearly vanished.'

differentiation.support: Backup tools (drawn base-10, number line) stay one tap away; fewer questions, same estimate-solve-check routine every time.
differentiation.stretch: Timed streak with no tools; add the two-step word problem and 70 − 23 (crossing the tens).

extension: Be the quiz master — the child writes three calculation questions (with answers!) for the tutor to solve, and catches the tutor's deliberate mistake.
assessmentEvidence: Child completes a mixed calculation set with mostly accurate, fluent answers, estimating first and using an inverse check.
revisitLater: Log the child's self-named weak strand and use it as the next lessons' warm-up; full mixed calculation retrieval returns before Unit 8.
